newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. May output rises 0.4 percent. [CORRECTED 16:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. May output rises 0.4 percent. [CORRECTED 16:05 GMT]

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Federal Reserve reported industrial output in May rose 0.4 percent and capacity utilization printed 83.7 (corrects from 83.9) percent.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.2 percent increase in industrial production and an 83.4 percent reading on capacity use.
RICK EGELTON, DEPUTY CHIEF ECONOMIST, HARRIS BANK/BANK OF MONTREAL: "We were expecting a number around 0.3 percent; it's a little higher at 0.4.
"It indicates that the economy in the U.S. is still moving ahead. We're looking at a slowdown in the second quarter, obviously, but this still seems to suggest there's some underlying momentum.
"We're still getting high levels of capacity utilization, so I think the threat on the price side in the future is still there," he added.
JOSEPH ABATE, ECONOMIST, LEHMAN GOVERNMENT SECURITIES INC.: "The 0.4 percent increase in IP was stronger than expected.
Abate continued: "Also, we had a bigger revision to April than what we were expecting. That was a negative for the (bond) market.

"The fact that the capacity utilization rate is now at the tightest level since September 1995 is also a negative for the market. A lot of the strength we're seeing in the IP numbers this morning is coming from a rebound in the motor vehicle assemblies, which were up 1.2 percent ... and in addition to that, there was strength in aircraft orders as well. The Fed is probably going to be on hold ... this number is moderately stronger ... but it's not excessively strong," he said.

KEN MAYLAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, KEYCORP: "Manufacturing is on a roll. The manufacturing sector is just doing Jim Dandy here. Is there any end in sight to production increases? Not that I can see. It's related to the inventory situation and the dynamic where inventories are judged to be very lean, which causes orders, which causes production, which causes jobs and income and ultimately spending. We are just on the sunny side of that inventory dynamic right now."
On Fed policy, he said, "The fact that inflation is low and not rising freezes them into no action."

WILLIAM GRIGGS, MANAGING DIRECTOR, GRIGGS & SANTOW INC: "The revisions are more noteworthy than the main numbers, but I wouldn't want to make too much of it. When industrial production came out in April, it was softer than expected. To some extent, it's painting a more realistic April picture.
"There's still no evidence of capacity producing inflation problems. This sort of information falls on fertile ground this morning because the market is nervous anyway.
"I think the most important thing this week will be the Beige Book, to get some idea of the thinking there."

RAPHAEL MARRONE, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL: "Utilities were down more than we thought, but mining was up a lot. Manufacturing was more or less in line with what we expected and we had an upward revision in April. That's consistent with our forecast of about 2-3/4 percent or 3.0 percent (growth) for the second quarter. Orders are relatively buoyant ... so there's quite a bit in the pipeline to fuel production. If consumers don't start spending from the low in the last three months, that could risk that production scenario, but we think consumer spending will snap back."

MICHAEL MORAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DAIWA SECURITIES AMERICA INC: "The industrial production number was a good one for the economy. It suggests that the manufacturing sector is continuing to hold its own and is putting in a good performance in the second quarter.

"We had a noticeable upward revision in April. Capacity utilization is at the upper end of the range. It's high enough to leave Fed officials concerned about resource utilization and inflation. I'd say the probability of a rate hike in July is low. The industrial production numbers are solid, but the CPI remains restrained. Final demand appears as though it's slowing, so I think the Fed will be patient and wait.

"The May industrial production report is partly an unwinding of strike effects. Another part of it is due to large backlogs of aircraft orders and the third area is high tech production, basically computers, remains strong."
